b: The Greek aetos also means vulture, and vultures gather over the dead (Matthew 24:28). Hosea 8:1 pictures an eagle over God's house with a trumpet to the lips, a fitting herald for the last three trumpets. The eagle is also one of the four living creatures (4:7).

why: The manuscripts are divided, and so are the editors. "Four" may have been added to answer the four angels of 9:14, or dropped because an altar's horns were known to be four (Exodus 27:2; Exodus 30:2–3). The Plain English Translation keeps to the SBLGNT; the meaning is the same either way.
b: Codex Sinaiticus as first written has neither form: it reads only "a voice of the gold altar," and a corrector added "one, from the horns" (Tischendorf's edition).

p: The Byzantine text has "myriads of myriads," a countless host, not an exact 200 million.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort
Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV "two hundred thousand thousand")

why: The rare word dismyriades, "double myriads," is the harder reading; copyists could easily turn it into the familiar "myriads of myriads" of 5:11 and Daniel 7:10.
b: The difference matters to readers who build on the exact figure (see the note on 9:16). The KJV's number is the same as the Plain English Translation's.

p: Modern editions read pharmaka, "potions, spells"; the Byzantine text and the KJV have pharmakeia, "sorceries."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort
Tregelles, the Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "sorceries")

why: Pharmakeia is the more common word and the one John uses at 18:23, so a copyist could easily have changed the rarer pharmaka to it. The meaning is nearly the same: both are about magic.

p: The Byzantine text says only "a mighty angel." The word "another" matters to the question of who this angel is.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Textus Receptus (KJV "another mighty angel")
Byzantine text

why: "Another" is in every edition except the Byzantine, and it links this angel to the mighty angel of 5:2.
b: Readers who argue that the angel is not Christ often point to "another": he is one more angel like the one in 5:2 (see the note on 10:1).

p: Here Codex Alexandrinus and the modern editions say simply "the scroll"; Codex Sinaiticus, the Byzantine text and the KJV make it "the little scroll," as in 10:2, 9 and 10.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) (βιβλαρίδιον); Byzantine text; Textus Receptus (KJV "the little book which is open")
readings.orig: τὸ βιβλιδάριον (Byzantine) / τὸ βιβλαρίδιον (TR) τὸ ἠνεῳγμένον

why: The plain word biblion is the harder reading in a chapter that otherwise says "little scroll"; copyists made it match.
b: Bauckham uses this verse to argue that the "little scroll" is the same scroll the Lamb took in chapter 5, now opened and given to John.

p: The Greek has only "saying," with no speaker. The KJV adds "and the angel stood."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the Byzantine text
A later corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); Textus Receptus (KJV "and the angel stood, saying")
readings.plain: and the angel stood there and said

why: The words are not in Codex Sinaiticus as first written, in the critical editions or in the Byzantine text. They look like a clarification that gives the loose participle "saying" a subject.

t: The Lord or the God of the earth?
p: The KJV has "the God of the earth." Every other text has "Lord," as in Zechariah 4:14.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV "the God of the earth")

why: "Lord" has the manuscript support and matches Zechariah 4:14, which John is echoing, where the olive trees stand by the Lord of all the earth.

p: In the Byzantine text John hears the voice; in the other texts the two witnesses hear it.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus as first written, Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Ephraemi and Codex P (as Tischendorf's 1865 edition notes); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Textus Receptus (KJV "they heard")
Byzantine text

why: The two forms differ by one letter. "I heard" is John's habit all through the book, which could easily draw a copyist to it; "they heard" fits the scene, where the call is spoken "to them."

p: The KJV has "the kingdoms of this world." The Greek manuscripts have one kingdom, the world's, which changes hands.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the Byzantine text
readings.en: the kingdom of the world has become

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord")
readings.en: the kingdoms of the world have become

why: The singular is in Codex Sinaiticus and in both the critical and the Byzantine editions; the plural is in none of the editions compared here except the Textus Receptus.
b: With the singular, the world is pictured as one kingdom, the one the dragon and the beast claim in chapters 12–13, and it changes hands. Handel's "Hallelujah" chorus, though its words come from the KJV, sings the singular: "The kingdom of this world."

p: Here, unlike 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8, God is only "who is and who was." The KJV adds "and art to come."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition), Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile), the Byzantine text; every modern edition
The Textus Receptus (KJV "which art, and wast, and art to come")
readings.orig: ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος
readings.en: who is and who was and who is coming
readings.plain: who is and who was and who is coming

why: Both of the oldest manuscripts have the shorter title, and so does the Byzantine text. The longer one copies the familiar threefold title of 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8, exactly the kind of change copyists made.
b: The shorter title is one of the book's most meaningful small details. At the seventh trumpet God is no longer "the one who is coming": he has come, and has taken up his reign. Bauckham, Beale and Koester all read the omission as deliberate. The same shortened title returns at 16:5.

p: The Byzantine text lacks "an earthquake" and reads "the ark of the covenant of the Lord."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Textus Receptus (KJV "and an earthquake")
Byzantine text

why: The modern editions keep the earthquake. The storm-signs grow at each step of the book (4:5; 8:5; 11:19; 16:18), and the shorter Byzantine list may have been made to match an earlier one.
b: The Byzantine text also has "the ark of the covenant of the Lord" for "the ark of his covenant"; the meaning is the same.

a: Woe to the earth and the sea
t: Woe to the earth, or to those who live on it?
p: The KJV's "inhabiters of the earth" comes from the Textus Receptus.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT; the Byzantine text has the same words in another case, and Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) reads "woe into the earth and the sea"
readings.orig: οὐαὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν
readings.en: woe to the earth and the sea
readings.plain: Woe to the earth and the sea

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea")
readings.orig: οὐαὶ τοῖς κατοικοῦσι τὴν γῆν καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν
readings.en: woe to those who live on the earth and the sea
readings.plain: Woe to those who live on the earth and the sea

why: The added words are in none of the editions compared here except the Textus Receptus; they look like a copy of the book's usual phrase "those who live on the earth" (as in 8:13).

p: The KJV adds "Christ" from the Textus Receptus.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile) and a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus, whose first copyist wrote "the testimony of God" (Tischendorf's edition); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT and the Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV "the testimony of Jesus Christ")

why: Even the Byzantine text has only "Jesus"; scribes often filled out the name.

p: One Greek letter decides whether the dragon or John stands by the sea. The KJV says "I stood."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s; Tischendorf's edition) and Codex Alexandrinus (400s; checked in the facsimile); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: καὶ ἐστάθη ἐπὶ τὴν ἄμμον τῆς θαλάσσης
readings.en: and he stood on the sand of the sea

readings.w: The Byzantine text; Textus Receptus (KJV "And I stood upon the sand of the sea")
readings.orig: καὶ ἐστάθην ἐπὶ τὴν ἄμμον τῆς θαλάσσης
readings.en: and I stood on the sand of the sea

why: The two oldest manuscripts have "he stood": the dragon, angry at the woman (12:17), takes his stand by the sea and calls up the beast. Copyists probably changed it to "I stood" to match the next words, "and I saw".
b: In NA28 and SBLGNT this clause is numbered 12:18. The KJV, and this site, which follows the KJV's verse numbers, place it at the start of 13:1, so chapter 12 here ends at 12:17. In the same verse the editions also differ between "names" (NA28, SBLGNT and the Byzantine text have the plural) and "name" of blasphemy (THGNT and the Textus Receptus, KJV "the name of blasphemy"); the meaning hardly changes.

p: The Byzantine text says the beast was given authority to make war for 42 months.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT; also the Textus Receptus (KJV "to continue")
The Byzantine text

why: "War" looks like an addition borrowed from 13:7 and 11:7. The KJV's "to continue" is a translation of the same short Greek.

a: his tent, those who live in heaven
t: His tent, that is, those in heaven?
p: The KJV adds "and," making the heavenly beings a separate target.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition), Codex Alexandrinus (facsimile) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: τὴν σκηνὴν αὐτοῦ, τοὺς ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ σκηνοῦντας
readings.en: his tent, those who dwell in heaven
readings.plain: his tent, those who live in heaven

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "and his tabernacle, and them that dwell in heaven")
readings.orig: τὴν σκηνὴν αὐτοῦ, καὶ τοὺς ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ σκηνοῦντας
readings.en: his tent, and those who dwell in heaven
readings.plain: his tent, and those who live in heaven

why: Without "and," God's tent is the people who live in heaven with him, a picture Revelation uses again (7:15; 21:3). The "and" is a later smoothing.

a: It was allowed to make war on the saints and to win the victory over them.
t: A sentence some old copies skip
p: Codex Alexandrinus, one of the two oldest manuscripts of the book, lacks this sentence, probably by a copying slip.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ ποιῆσαι πόλεμον μετὰ τῶν ἁγίων καὶ νικῆσαι αὐτούς
readings.en: and it was given to it to make war with the saints and to conquer them
readings.plain: It was allowed to make war on the saints and to win the victory over them.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile)

why: The sentence and the next one both begin "and it was given to it" (καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ). A copyist's eye could easily jump from the first to the second and leave out the words between. The sentence also repeats Daniel 7:21, which fits John's use of Daniel in this chapter.

a: If anyone is headed for captivity, into captivity they go.
t: Going into captivity, or leading others into it?
p: The KJV's "He that leadeth into captivity" comes from a different Greek text. This variant goes with the next one in the same verse.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: εἴ τις εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν, εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν ὑπάγει
readings.en: if anyone is for captivity, into captivity he goes
readings.plain: If anyone is headed for captivity, into captivity they go.

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "He that leadeth into captivity shall go into captivity")
readings.orig: εἴ τις αἰχμαλωσίαν συνάγει, εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν ὑπάγει
readings.en: if anyone gathers into captivity, into captivity he goes
readings.plain: If anyone leads others into captivity, into captivity they go.

readings.w: The Byzantine text
readings.en: if anyone holds captives, he goes away
readings.plain: If anyone holds others captive, they will go away.

why: The followed reading repeats Jeremiah 15:2 (compare Jeremiah 43:11): those meant for captivity will go into captivity. The other forms turn the saying into a rule of payback, which looks like a later attempt to make the hard saying easier.

a: If anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword they must be killed.
t: Killed by the sword, or killing with it?
p: Codex Sinaiticus, the Byzantine text and the KJV read "he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword." This goes with the variant before it.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); NA28, SBLGNT
readings.orig: εἴ τις ἐν μαχαίρῃ ἀποκτανθῆναι, αὐτὸν ἐν μαχαίρῃ ἀποκτανθῆναι
readings.en: if anyone is to be killed with the sword, he is to be killed with the sword
readings.plain: If anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword they must be killed.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) (with the present "kills") and the Byzantine text; Textus Receptus (KJV "he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword")
readings.orig: εἴ τις ἐν μαχαίρᾳ ἀποκτενεῖ, δεῖ αὐτὸν ἐν μαχαίρᾳ ἀποκτανθῆναι
readings.en: if anyone will kill with the sword, he must be killed with the sword
readings.plain: If anyone kills with the sword, by the sword they must be killed.

why: NA28 and SBLGNT follow Alexandrinus: its Greek is rough, which is why copyists would smooth it, and it keeps the pattern of Jeremiah 15:2 and the first half of the verse. Read this way, the verse tells the saints to accept suffering. The other reading, close to Jesus' words in Matthew 26:52, warns them not to take up the sword. Both lead to the same call: "This is where the saints show their endurance."
b: Some editions (Westcott-Hort, Tregelles and the Tyndale House Greek New Testament) print "must" (δεῖ) in the second half, with the Byzantine text. The 13:9–10 card on this chapter page gives the setting.

p: The KJV makes the name a second, separate option.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (facsimile) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: τὸ χάραγμα, τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θηρίου
readings.en: the mark, the name of the beast

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "the mark, or the name of the beast")
readings.orig: τὸ χάραγμα, ἢ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θηρίου
readings.en: the mark, or the name of the beast
readings.plain: the mark, or the beast's name

why: In this text the mark is the beast's name or its number, not a third thing beside them.

p: The oldest surviving copy of this verse reads 616. Nearly all others read 666.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and Codex Alexandrinus (facsimile), both in words; the Byzantine text; Irenaeus; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT; the Textus Receptus (as a numeral, χξϛʹ)

P115 (P.Oxy. 4499, a fragment from about AD 300 and the oldest surviving copy of the verse) and Codex Ephraemi (400s), both as reported by Daniel B. Wallace; copies known to Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.1)
Minuscule 2344, a later manuscript (listed in published summaries of the variants)

why: 666 has by far the widest support, and Irenaeus, about AD 180, said it stood in all the good and ancient copies, while he knew of copies with 616 and thought them a mistake. Still, 616 is very old, and it fits a known explanation: "Nero Caesar" in Hebrew letters adds up to 666 when spelled נרון קסר and to 616 when spelled the Latin way, נרו קסר. Many scholars think a copyist who knew the Nero reading adjusted the number to the Latin spelling.
b: On what "a human number" means, see the note on those words and the 13:16–18 card.

a: his name and the name of his Father
p: The KJV has only "his Father's name."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: his name and the name of his Father
readings.plain: his name and the name of his Father

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "having his Father's name written in their foreheads")

why: The shorter reading is in none of the editions compared here except the Textus Receptus; the eye could skip from the first "name" to the second. The KJV also says "a Lamb," where the Greek has "the Lamb."

p: The critical editions and the KJV have "as it were" (ὡς); Codex Sinaiticus and the Byzantine text do not.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT; Textus Receptus (KJV "they sung as it were a new song")
readings.en: they sing as it were a new song

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text

why: The Plain English Translation follows its base text, SBLGNT. "As it were" fits John's way of describing what he hears ("like the roar of many waters," 14:2), and a copyist may have dropped it to match 5:9. The evidence is divided.

p: The KJV adds "before the throne of God," which none of the other editions has.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT (the Byzantine text adds "for")
Textus Receptus (KJV "for they are without fault before the throne of God")
readings.orig: ἄμωμοι γάρ εἰσιν ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου τοῦ θεοῦ
readings.en: for they are without fault before the throne of God
readings.plain: For they are without blemish before the throne of God.

why: The added words are an expansion, perhaps from Jude 24, where God presents believers "without blemish" before his glory.

p: The Byzantine text has the cry once; the KJV has it twice and adds "that great city."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT; Textus Receptus
The Byzantine text; a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus, who supplied the missing cry (its first copyist skipped it; Tischendorf's edition)

why: The double cry follows Isaiah 21:9, which this verse quotes, and 18:2 repeats it.
b: The Textus Receptus also reads "Babylon is fallen, is fallen, that great city" (KJV), adding "city" (ἡ πόλις); none of the other editions has it.

p: The KJV adds "and over his mark."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
Textus Receptus (KJV "and over his image, and over his mark")
readings.orig: ἐκ τῆς εἰκόνος αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ χαράγματος αὐτοῦ
readings.en: over its image and over its mark
readings.plain: over its image, over its mark

why: "His mark" is a natural addition from 13:16–17 and 14:9; Codex Sinaiticus and the critical and Byzantine editions lack it.

t: King of the nations, of the ages, or of the saints?
p: Here the Plain English Translation departs from its base text, SBLGNT, which reads "King of the ages." The KJV says "King of saints."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile), a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, THGNT, Tregelles
Codex Sinaiticus as first written (Tischendorf's edition); SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort
The Textus Receptus (KJV "thou King of saints")

why: The song draws on Jeremiah 10:7, "King of the nations," and goes straight on to "All the nations will come and worship" (15:4), so "nations" fits the context; it is in Alexandrinus and the Byzantine text, and NA28 prints it. "King of the ages" is what Sinaiticus first read and is a real possibility; it may have come in from 1 Timothy 1:17. "Saints" is in none of the editions compared here except the Textus Receptus.

t: Dressed in linen, or in stone?
p: Codex Alexandrinus says the angels were dressed in pure, bright stone.

readings.w: The Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus (Codex Sinaiticus, in Tischendorf's edition, has a related form: "pure, bright linen garments")
Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile), which reads ΛΙΘΟΝ; some Latin Vulgate texts (lapide; the Clementine Vulgate has lino, "linen"); Westcott-Hort, Tregelles

why: In Greek capitals the two words differ by one letter (ΛΙΝΟΝ, ΛΙΘΟΝ), and most editors judge "stone" a copying slip. But it is the harder reading and the reading of Alexandrinus: some compare the king of Tyre dressed in precious stones (Ezekiel 28:13). Westcott-Hort and Tregelles print it; the other editions set it aside.

a: the one who is and who was
p: No known Greek manuscript has "and shalt be." It came from the editor Theodore Beza.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, the Byzantine text
readings.orig: ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν, ὁ ὅσιος
readings.en: who is and who was, the Holy One
readings.plain: the one who is and who was

readings.w: Theodore Beza, who proposed it in his Latin translation and notes (checked in his 1588 edition), saying he had restored it from an old manuscript; the Textus Receptus behind the KJV follows him (KJV "O Lord, which art, and wast, and shalt be")
readings.orig: ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐσόμενος
readings.en: who is and who was and who will be
readings.plain: the one who is and who was and who will be

why: Beza argued in his notes that "the Holy One" broke the pattern of 1:4 and 1:8 and that John must have written "who will be"; he claimed an old manuscript for it, but none is known today, and the Textus Receptus and the KJV followed him. The Greek manuscripts and editions read "who is and who was, the Holy One." The missing third part is deliberate on John's part; see the note on "and who was."
b: In Beza's 1588 edition the Greek column itself still prints καὶ ὁ ὅσιος, "and the Holy One," after "O Lord" (Κύριε); "who will be" appears in his Latin translation and his note.

t: The altar speaks, or someone at it?
p: The KJV has "another out of the altar," a voice from the altar rather than the altar itself.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
Textus Receptus (KJV "I heard another out of the altar say")
readings.orig: ἤκουσα ἄλλου ἐκ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου λέγοντος
readings.en: I heard another from the altar saying
readings.plain: another voice from the altar say

why: The Textus Receptus smooths a bold image. In the Greek the altar itself, where the martyrs' souls cried out (6:9–10), answers that God's judgments are just.

a: the kings of the whole world
t: "Of the earth and of the whole world"
p: The KJV adds "of the earth."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT

readings.plain: the kings of the whole world

readings.en: the kings of the earth and of the whole world
readings.plain: the kings of the earth and of the whole world

why: "The kings of the earth" is a familiar phrase in Revelation (17:2; 18:3), so "of the earth" was easily added.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say "out of the temple of heaven."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition, "out of the temple of God"); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
The Byzantine text; Textus Receptus (KJV "out of the temple of heaven")
readings.plain: out of the temple of heaven

why: The meaning is the same, since the temple is in heaven (15:5); "of heaven" spells it out.

p: NA28 reads the singular, "since a human being came to be on the earth," perhaps a hint at Adam.

readings.w: SBLGNT, the Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "since men were upon the earth")
NA28 (and Tregelles)
readings.en: since a human being came to be
readings.plain: since a human being came to be

why: The Plain English Translation follows its base text, SBLGNT. The difference is small: either way, no earthquake like it has happened in all human history (compare Daniel 12:1).

p: The KJV's "and yet is" comes from the printed Textus Receptus, not from the main Greek manuscripts.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s; it adds "again," as Tischendorf's 1865 edition shows) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT
Textus Receptus (KJV "and yet is")

why: The manuscripts support "will be present." "And yet is" is easily explained as a misreading of the same letters: KAIPARESTAI (and will be present) taken as KAIPERESTIN (although it is).
b: The difference matters. "Was, and is not, and will be here" is a parody of God, "who is, who was, and who is coming" (1:4, 8): the beast fakes a coming of its own. "And yet is" loses the parody.

a: a prison for every unclean bird, a prison for every unclean and hated animal
t: A haunt of unclean birds, and of unclean animals?
p: The Plain English Translation follows its base text with three "prisons." Many manuscripts have two, and the KJV joins "hated" to the bird.

readings.orig: φυλακὴ παντὸς ὀρνέου ἀκαθάρτου καὶ φυλακὴ παντὸς θηρίου ἀκαθάρτου καὶ μεμισημένου

readings.plain: a prison for every unclean bird, a prison for every unclean and hated animal

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (checked in Tischendorf's edition), the Byzantine text; Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "a cage of every unclean and hateful bird")
readings.orig: φυλακὴ παντὸς ὀρνέου ἀκαθάρτου καὶ μεμισημένου
readings.en: a prison of every unclean and hated bird
readings.plain: a prison for every unclean and hated bird

why: The site's base text, the SBLGNT, prints the longer form, and NA28 prints it too. The repeated words "a prison of every unclean..." make it easy for a copyist's eye to jump from one to the next and drop a line; on the other hand, a scribe could have added the third line to round out the picture of Isaiah 13:21–22 and 34:11–14. Tyndale House prints the shorter form.
b: The cry "Fallen, fallen" is doubled in NA28, SBLGNT and the Textus Receptus, as in Isaiah 21:9; Codex Sinaiticus and the Byzantine text have "Fallen" once. Codex Alexandrinus (facsimile) has yet another form: a prison for every unclean and hated spirit and a prison for every unclean and hated beast, with no bird line.

p: The Plain English Translation follows NA28 ("have drunk") against its own base text, the SBLGNT ("have fallen"). The two Greek words differ by one letter.

readings.w: NA28; the Textus Receptus also has "drunk" (πέπωκε; KJV)
Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) (πεπτώκασιν), Codex Alexandrinus and Ephraemi (πέπτωκαν, as reported by S. P. Tregelles), the Byzantine text; SBLGNT

why: The better-attested reading is "have fallen (by the wine)," and the SBLGNT prints it. The Plain English Translation follows NA28's "have drunk" because it fits the picture the book has already drawn: Babylon "made all the nations drink" her wine (14:8), and those who live on the earth "were made drunk" with it (17:2). The two words differ by one letter (pepōkan, pepṭōkan), and "fallen" may have come in from "Fallen, fallen" one verse earlier. This is a close call, and readers should know the main manuscripts say "fallen."

p: The Greek has no object. The KJV's "as she rewarded you" adds "you" from the Textus Receptus.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT
Textus Receptus (KJV "even as she rewarded you")
readings.plain: as she herself has repaid you

why: "You" is in the Textus Receptus, not in Codex Sinaiticus or the critical and Byzantine editions; it reads like an explanation added to fill the gap.

p: The KJV lacks "spice" (amomum), which Codex Sinaiticus as first written and the critical editions have.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand; a corrector removed it, as Tischendorf's edition shows); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
The Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "cinnamon, and odours")

why: The two words end alike (kinnamōmon, amōmon), so a copyist's eye could easily skip from one to the other and drop the second. Amomum was a costly fragrant plant used for ointments.

p: The Plain English Translation follows NA28 and Tyndale House in reading "our"; the SBLGNT and the KJV lack it.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus ("God our Lord," checked in Tischendorf's edition), the Byzantine text; NA28 (in brackets), Tyndale House GNT
SBLGNT; Textus Receptus (KJV "the Lord God omnipotent")

why: "Our" has the support of Sinaiticus and the Byzantine text, and it matches "our God" in 19:1 and 19:5; NA28 and Tyndale House print it. The SBLGNT leaves it out. The meaning hardly changes.

a: wears a robe dipped in blood
p: Codex Sinaiticus and Westcott-Hort say the robe was "sprinkled" with blood.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "dipped in blood")
readings.plain: wears a robe dipped in blood

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand περιρεραμμένον, a corrector περιρεραντισμένον; Tischendorf's edition); Westcott-Hort (ῥεραντισμένον)
readings.en: a garment sprinkled (all over) with blood
readings.plain: wears a robe sprinkled with blood

why: "Dipped" is the harder word and best explains the others: copyists seem to have softened it, or brought it closer to the spattered garments of Isaiah 63:3 and the sprinkling of blood in the Law. Even within Sinaiticus a corrector changed the spelling, a sign of later tinkering.
b: The choice touches the debate in the note on this verse: a robe "dipped" in blood before the battle is soaked through, which many read as the rider's own blood.

a: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were finished.
p: Codex Sinaiticus leaves out the first sentence of 20:5.

readings.w: The Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: οἱ λοιποὶ τῶν νεκρῶν οὐκ ἔζησαν ἄχρι τελεσθῇ τὰ χίλια ἔτη.
readings.en: the rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were completed
readings.plain: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were finished.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition)

why: The sentence is in every edition. Its loss is easy to explain: 20:4 and the sentence both end with "a thousand years" (chilia etē), so a copyist's eye could jump from the first ending to the second.
b: The sentence matters for the millennium debate. Without it there is no explicit second group raised after the thousand years, and premillennial readers lean on it for two resurrections a thousand years apart. Amillennial readers point out that the KJV and most Bibles print it, and that "came to life" can be read in more than one way (see the notes on 20:4 and 20:5).

The Byzantine text; Tregelles

readings.plain: came down from heaven, from God

readings.w: A corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (its first copyist skipped the whole passage; checked in Tischendorf's edition); Textus Receptus (KJV "came down from God out of heaven")

why: "From God" turns up in different places in different manuscripts, which is the usual sign of an addition. The short reading also matches the fire that came down from heaven in 2 Kings 1:10–12, which the verse echoes.

t: "The lake of fire" at the end?

readings.plain: This is the second death, the lake of fire.

why: The closing words are in Codex Sinaiticus and every edition except the Textus Receptus; the Textus Receptus seems to have lost them because the sentence before also ends with "the lake of fire."

p: The two oldest manuscripts have the plural, "peoples," which breaks the old formula "my people."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); NA28, SBLGNT; also the Textus Receptus
The Byzantine text; the KJV's "his people" (which may simply render the plural)

why: The plural is the harder reading: the familiar promise is "you will be my people," singular (Leviticus 26:12; Ezekiel 37:27), and copyists would tend to bring the verse back to it. The plural makes the point that the people of God now come from many nations (5:9; 7:9).

a: God himself will be with them and be their God
p: The Plain English Translation follows NA28 and Tyndale House in printing "and be their God." The SBLGNT, Sinaiticus and the Byzantine text lack it.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile); NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "and be their God")
readings.orig: καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς μετ’ αὐτῶν ἔσται αὐτῶν θεός
readings.en: and God himself will be with them, their God
readings.plain: God himself will be with them and be their God

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (checked in Tischendorf's edition), the Byzantine text; SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς μετ’ αὐτῶν ἔσται
readings.en: and God himself will be with them
readings.plain: God himself will be with them

why: A close call. The words could have been added to complete the covenant formula ("I will be your God"), or dropped because they seemed to repeat "with them" (meta autōn ... autōn). NA28 and Tyndale House print them; the site's base text, the SBLGNT, does not. The Plain English Translation keeps them, so this entry marks a place where it leaves the SBLGNT.

t: "It has happened," "I have become," or "It is done"?
p: Three forms of one Greek verb, and three meanings.

readings.orig: Γέγοναν. ἐγώ τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ
readings.en: They have happened. I am the Alpha and the Omega
readings.plain: It has all happened. I am the Alpha and the Omega

readings.orig: Γέγονα τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ

readings.plain: I have become the Alpha and the Omega

readings.plain: It is done. I am the Alpha and the Omega

why: "They have happened" (plural) is unusual and the hardest to explain as a copyist's change; the singular forms look like smoothings. It refers back to "these words" of 21:5: everything God promised has come to pass. Compare the single word from the throne in 16:17.

p: The KJV's "that great city, the holy Jerusalem" follows the later text.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition); NA28, SBLGNT
The Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "that great city, the holy Jerusalem")
readings.orig: τὴν πόλιν τὴν μεγάλην τὴν ἁγίαν Ἰερουσαλήμ
readings.en: the great city, the holy Jerusalem
readings.plain: the great city, the holy Jerusalem

why: In Revelation "the great city" is Babylon (17:18; 18:10). Codex Sinaiticus and the critical editions call the new Jerusalem "the holy city" only (as in 21:2); "great" was probably added by copyists who knew the phrase.

t: "The nations of those who are saved"?
p: The KJV narrows "the nations" to "the nations of them which are saved."

The Textus Receptus (KJV "the nations of them which are saved shall walk")

readings.plain: The nations of those who are saved will walk

a: Let the righteous go on doing righteousness
p: The KJV's "let him be righteous still" comes from the Textus Receptus.

readings.en: let the righteous still do righteousness
readings.plain: Let the righteous go on doing righteousness

a: Blessed are those who wash their robes
p: The KJV's "Blessed are they that do his commandments" follows the Byzantine text.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile), with the Latin Vulgate (qui lavant stolas suas); NA28, SBLGNT
readings.orig: μακάριοι οἱ πλύνοντες τὰς στολὰς αὐτῶν
readings.en: blessed are those who wash their robes
readings.plain: Blessed are those who wash their robes

readings.w: The Byzantine text; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: μακάριοι οἱ ποιοῦντες τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: blessed are those who do his commandments
readings.plain: Blessed are those who do his commandments

why: The two oldest Greek manuscripts have "wash their robes," which ties back to 7:14 ("they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb"). Written in capitals with no spaces, as scribes wrote, the two readings look alike: ΠΛΥΝΟΝΤΕΣΤΑΣΣΤΟΛΑΣ and ΠΟΙΟΥΝΤΕΣΤΑΣΕΝΤΟΛΑΣ. A tired copyist could slip, and keeping the commandments of God is a theme John returns to (12:17; 14:12).
b: The difference shapes the verse. "Wash their robes" makes entry a gift received; "do his commandments" makes it faithful obedience. Revelation holds both together elsewhere (12:17; 14:12; 22:7).

p: The KJV's "book of life" goes back to Erasmus, who translated the last verses of the book into Greek from the Latin.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (Tischendorf's edition) and the Byzantine text; NA28, SBLGNT
Erasmus's Greek New Testament (1516), which supplied 22:16–21 by translating from the Latin; Textus Receptus (KJV "out of the book of life")

why: None of the Greek editions compared here reads "book" except the Textus Receptus. Latin texts differ here between ligno ("tree") and libro ("book"); Erasmus's Greek follows "book," and the Textus Receptus kept it.
b: When Erasmus prepared the first Greek New Testament to be published (1516), his only manuscript of Revelation was a twelfth-century copy with the commentary of Andrew of Caesarea (now called minuscule 2814). It had lost its last leaf, with 22:16–21. Erasmus filled the gap by translating the Latin back into Greek, and some of his words stayed in the Textus Receptus behind the KJV. Two reach the KJV here: "book of life" in this verse, and "with you all" in 22:21. Other wording in these verses also differs from every Greek manuscript (for example, the Textus Receptus has ἐλθέ for ἔρχου, "come," in 22:17).

p: The last words have four forms in the manuscripts, and Codex Alexandrinus lacks "Amen."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (checked in the British Museum facsimile), without "Amen"; NA28, SBLGNT
Codex Sinaiticus (checked in Tischendorf's edition); Tyndale House GNT (Westcott-Hort print "with the saints" without "Amen")
The Byzantine text, which also reads "the Lord Jesus Christ"
Textus Receptus (KJV "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen"), from Erasmus's back-translation

why: The SBLGNT and NA28 follow Codex Alexandrinus, which has the short "with all" and no "Amen." "Amen" is the kind of word copyists added at the end of a book read in church, and "the saints" may come from the usual close of letters. Tyndale House follows Sinaiticus. The KJV's "with you all" has almost no Greek support: it comes from Erasmus's Latin-based Greek (see 22:19).
